 2       NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION ("COMMISSION")?

 3   A   Yes. I have been involved in prior proceedings before this Commission and have

 4       presented testimony in many of those proceedings.


 5   Q   PLEASE       DESCRIBE        YOUR      EDUCATIONAL            BACKGROUND             AND

 6       EXPERIENCE.

 7   A   This information is included in Appendix A to my testimony.


 8   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 9   A   I reviewed EPE’s requested overall rate of return including return on equity, an

10       appropriate and cost-effective ratemaking capital structure, and embedded debt

11       component costs. I also reviewed EPE's proposed Large Load Tariffs.


12   Q   DOES THE FACT THAT YOU DID NOT ADDRESS EVERY ISSUE RAISED

13       IN EPE’S TESTIMONY MEAN THAT YOU AGREE WITH THE COMPANY’S

14       TESTIMONY ON THOSE ISSUES?

15   A   No. It merely reflects that I did not choose to address all those issues. It should not be

16       read as an endorsement of, or agreement with, EPE’s position on such issues. In

17       addition, other parties may offer reasonable adjustments to EPE’s revenue requirement

18       that I have not addressed in my Direct Testimony.

 1   Q   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS

 2       ON RETURN ON EQUITY.

 3   A   I recommend that the Commission, consistent with long-standing and accepted legal

 4       principles, approve a return on equity that reflects EPE’s investment risk and charges

 5       customers rates that are as low and as competitive as possible while also fairly

 6       compensating EPE and maintaining its access to capital, financial integrity, and credit

 7       standing. I have carefully weighed these objectives of financial integrity for EPE and

 8       rate affordability for customers in arriving at my recommended overall rate of return,

 9       which is composed of the following:

10          1) I recommend the Commission award a return on common equity within
11             my recommended range of 9.15% to 9.75% with an approximate
12             midpoint of 9.45%;

13          2) I recommend the Commission authorize a balanced ratemaking capital
14             structure composed of 51.0% common equity and 49.0% long-term
15             debt. This ratemaking capital structure is more cost effective than the
16             one proposed by the Company and will support EPE's credit rating and
17             financial integrity. This ratemaking capital structure is comparable to
18             the last authorized capital structure but reflects an increase to the
19             common equity ratio relative to the approved capital structure in EPE’s
20             last New Mexico rate case; and

21          3) I recommend an overall rate of return of 7.48% for EPE as shown on
22             Exhibit MPG-1.

23              My recommended overall rate of return relative to EPE’s requested rate of return

24       will lower the claimed revenue deficiency in this case by approximately $8.5 million.

25       This overall revenue requirement impact is based on my proposed adjustments: (1) to

26       reject the Company’s proposal to increase the ratemaking capital structure equity ratio

27       to 55.5% and approve a capital structure with common equity ratio of 51.00%, which

28       lowers the claimed revenue deficiency by $2.7 million, and (2) to lower the authorized
                                                         Public Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman

 1       return on equity to 9.45% from the Company’s requested equity return of 10.70%, which

 2       decreases the requested revenue requirement by an additional $5.9 million.

 3                 I will also respond to EPE witness Nelson’s recommended return on equity range

 4       of 10.00% to 11.40% and the Company’s proposed return on equity of 10.70%. 1 I

 5       demonstrate that the Company’s proposed return of 10.70% overstates a fair and

 6       reasonable return on equity for EPE in this case. Setting rates based on an above-market

 7       return on equity, as proposed by Ms. Nelson would economically harm customers and

 8       would fail to protect customers by setting rates above a just and reasonable amount.

 9                 Finally, I respond to the Company's proposed new rate offerings for large load

10       customers: High Load Factor Service, Rate 50, and Large Load Service Rate 51. I do

11       not take issue with implementing these rates for new customers, but I do recommend

12       that customers that are currently being served on existing rate schedules retain the right

13       to stay on their rate schedule if they so choose.


14   Q   HOW WILL YOUR TESTIMONY ON RATE OF RETURN BE ORGANIZED?

15   A   First, I discuss observable market evidence that outlines how regulatory decisions and

16       authorized returns on equity have supported regulated utilities’ credit standing, access

17       to capital, and stock price valuations. This observable market data is important evidence

18       of what the market has perceived to be fair ratemaking treatment for regulated utilities,

19       while also ensuring that utilities’ rates are as affordable as possible, all of which is

20       necessary to support utilities’ financial integrity and credit standing.

 8   A     In this section, I will provide observable market evidence and credit metrics to assess

11         capital.     I also comment on market-based models used to estimate the current

12         market-required rate of return that investors demand to assume the risk of an investment

13         similar to EPE’s.

 1   Q   HAVE UTILITIES BEEN ABLE TO ACCESS EXTERNAL CAPITAL TO

 2       SUPPORT CAPITAL EXPENDITURE PROGRAMS?

 3   A   Yes. Utilities have enjoyed robust access to capital markets under favorable terms and

 4       costs. This access to capital is in recognition of the returns that regulatory commissions

 5       have found to be fair and reasonable. The Regulatory Research Associates’ (“RRA”)

 6       April 14, 2026, Utility Capital Expenditures Report, RRA Financial Focus, made

 7       several relevant comments about utility investments generally:

 8              •   The RRA forecasts approximately $1.3 trillion of aggregate capital
 9                  expenditures for US energy utilities between 2026 and 2030 as
10                  companies seek to modernize infrastructure and add generation
11                  capacity in response to heightened energy demand from large-load
12                  customers, particularly data centers that support AI, digital services
13                  and cloud infrastructure. Data centers, along with other large
14                  industrial loads such as new manufacturing facilities, are fueling the
15                  need for new power supplies through 2035, adding 374 TWh of
16                  energy demand and over 45 GW of peak load, according to analysts
17                  at S&P Global Energy CERA.

18              •   RRA's updated 2026 capex forecast represents an approximate 29%
19                  increase from roughly $200 billion spent in 2025. Aggregate energy
20                  utility investments are now projected at $259.122 billion in 2026,
21                  $275.592 billion in 2027 and $276.921 billion in 2028 — an
22                  approximately 9% increase over 2026–28 forecast spending levels in
23                  RRA's December 2025 capex forecast. Within the smaller investor-
24                  owned water utility sector, total capex is projected to grow
25                  approximately 16% in 2026 to $6.947 billion, from $6.003 billion in
26                  2025, continuing a trend of double-digit annual capex growth rates.

27              •   The elevated pace of capital expenditures over the next several
28                  years will require a commensurate level of regulatory engagement to
29                  secure timely cost recovery; as such, Regulatory Research Associates
30                  anticipates ongoing elevated rate case activity across the sector, with
31                  a focus on balancing the need for significant infrastructure
32                  investment      against    customer affordability      considerations.

 3   Q   HAVE REGULATED UTILITY EQUITY VALUATIONS SUPPORTED

 4       ACCESS TO EQUITY CAPITAL?

 5   A   Yes. Utility valuation metrics continue to demonstrate that utilities can sell new stock

 6       at robust market prices, which illustrates that utilities can access equity capital under

 7       reasonable terms and conditions and at relatively low cost.

 8               As shown on my Exhibit MPG-2, utility valuation metrics show robust valuation

 9       of utility securities more recently compared to the historical period stretching back

10       to 2002. Specifically, The Value Line Investment Survey (“Value Line”) tracks and

11       projects various valuation metrics related to regulated utility securities, as well as certain

12       non-regulated companies followed by Value Line.              These valuation metrics are

13       considered by market participants in assessing the investment risk characteristics of

14       individual company stocks and industries and are used by market participants to derive

15       their required rates of return for making investments. All of these valuation metrics for

16       utility stocks indicate robust valuations of utility stocks, which in turn support my

17       finding that utilities’ cost of capital is low by historical comparison and utilities are

18       producing competitive returns.

19               For example, the Value Line electric utility industry price-to-earnings ratio of

20       18.99x for 2026 exceeds the 25-year average price-to-earnings ratio. A consistently

21       strong price-to-earnings ratio indicates stock price valuations are stable, which supports

22       utilities’ access to external equity markets.

 1   Q       HOW SHOULD THE COMMISSION USE THIS MARKET INFORMATION IN

 2           ASSESSING A FAIR RETURN FOR EPE?

 3   A       Observable market evidence is quite clear that capital market costs are relatively low. As

 4           authorized returns have fluctuated around the mid-9% range over the past five years,

 5           utilities continue to have access to large amounts of external capital while funding large

 6           capital programs. Furthermore, utilities’ investment-grade credit ratings are stable due to

 7           supportive regulatory treatment.     The Commission should carefully weigh all this

 8           important observable market evidence in assessing a fair return on equity for EPE.

10   Q        ARE THE MONETARY POLICY DECISIONS AND ACTIONS OF THE

11            FEDERAL RESERVE (“FED”), AND OF THE FEDERAL RESERVE

12            SYSTEM’S FEDERAL OPEN MARKET COMMITTEE (“FOMC”), KNOWN

13            TO MARKET PARTICIPANTS, AND IS IT REASONABLE TO BELIEVE

14            THOSE DECISIONS AND ACTIONS ARE REFLECTED IN THE MARKET’S

15            VALUATION OF BOTH DEBT AND EQUITY SECURITIES?

16   A        Yes. The Fed has been transparent in its efforts to support the economy to achieve

17            maximum employment and to manage long-term inflation to around a 2% level. In a

18            September 16, 2026, press release, the Fed noted that economic activity has been

19            expanding at a solid pace despite the elevated geopolitical uncertainty. The Fed also

20            stated that the productivity growth and capital investments are strong, while

21            unemployment rate remains stable. Meanwhile, inflation remains slightly elevated

 5       their rate base grows rapidly, which in turn accelerates earnings growth. Once a major

 6       construction cycle is completed or levels off, growth in the utility rate base slows and

 7       its earnings growth slows from an abnormally high three- to five-year rate to a lower

 8       sustainable growth rate. The electric utility industry is currently in the middle of a major

 9       construction cycle, driven by unprecedented growth in electric demand, environmental

10       improvements to resources, and infrastructure modernization. Thus, the multi-stage

11       DCF model is particularly appropriate in current market conditions.

 4   III.G. Capital Asset Pricing Model (“CAPM”)

 5   Q     PLEASE DESCRIBE THE CAPM.

 6   A     The CAPM method of analysis is based upon the theory that the market-required rate of

 7         return for a security is equal to the risk-free rate, plus a risk premium associated with

 8         the specific security. This relationship between risk and return can be expressed

 9         mathematically as follows:

10                Ri = Rf + Bi x (Rm - Rf) where:

11                        Ri =    Required return for stock i
12                        Rf =    Risk-free rate
13                        Rm =    Expected return for the market portfolio
14                        Bi =    Beta - Measure of the risk for stock

15                The stock-specific risk term in the above equation is beta. Beta represents the

16         investment risk that cannot be diversified away when the security is held in a diversified

17         portfolio. When stocks are held in a diversified portfolio, stock-specific risks can be

18         eliminated by balancing the portfolio with securities that react in the opposite direction

19         to firm-specific risk factors (e.g., business cycle, competition, product mix, and

20         production limitations).

21                Risks that cannot be eliminated when held in a diversified portfolio are

22         non-diversifiable risks. Non-diversifiable risks are related to the market and referred to

23         as systematic risks. In contrast, risks that can be eliminated by diversification are
                                                                 Public Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman
                                                                               NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                                                                                                      Page 65


 1       non-systematic risks.          In a broad sense, systematic risks are market risks and

 2       non-systematic risks are business risks. The CAPM theory suggests the market will not

 3       compensate investors for assuming risks that can be diversified away. Therefore, the

 4       only risk investors will be compensated for are systematic, or non-diversifiable, risks.

 5       The beta is a measure of these systematic, or non-diversifiable risks.
